examples.label: Add an unexpected 'confirmed'/'admin' parameter to the request
Rails equivalent - inject admin:true into the user object

notes: The winning move is adding a parameter the form never sent (confirmed=true, admin=true, role=admin) - diff the object model against the form. Best found by reading source or guessing framework conventions.

recommended.note: Another application-logic web vuln in this module.

name: Web Mass Assignment - Inject Extra Parameters
description: Frameworks that bind all request params to model fields let you set attributes the form never exposed. Add a parameter like confirmed=true or admin=true to a registration/update request to self-approve or escalate.

variations.command: curl -s -X PATCH http://<target>/api/v1/<endpoint> -H "Authorization: Bearer <jwt_token>" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"id": "<object_id>", "isExemptedFromMarketplaceFee": 1}' | jq

defense.why_it_works: Mass assignment vulnerabilities occur when a web framework automatically binds HTTP request parameters to model attributes without filtering. An attacker adds extra parameters to a registration request (e.g., 'confirmed=True', 'admin=true') that the framework maps to privileged model fields.
defense.prerequisites: Web framework with automatic parameter binding without allowlist enforcement. A registration or profile update endpoint.
defense.impact: Privilege escalation: attacker registers as admin, bypasses approval workflows, or sets internal-only fields (confirmed, role, is_admin) from a normal registration form.
defense.detection: Registration or update requests containing unexpected parameters not in the application's HTML form. New admin user created via registration. Parameter anomaly detection in WAF.
defense.artifacts: Web server access log (POST /register with extra parameters) | Application audit log (admin user created via registration) | Database: user record with admin flag set by attacker
defense.prevention: Use allowlists for parameter binding -- explicitly specify which fields are user-settable. In Rails: strong_parameters. In Flask: explicitly extract only required fields from request.form. Never bind all request parameters to a model.
defense.misconfiguration: Flask registration endpoint maps all form fields to DB columns, including 'confirmed' (approval status) which should only be set by administrators.
defense.secure_config:
# Secure Flask -- hardcode non-user-settable fields
@app.route('/register', methods=['POST'])
def register():
    username = request.form['username']
    password = request.form['password']
    confirmed = False   # always False -- never from user input
    cur.execute('insert into users values(?,?,?)', (username, password, confirmed))

# Rails: params.require(:user).permit(:username, :email, :password)
defense.evasion: Add parameter in URL query string instead of POST body. Use JSON body if endpoint accepts both. Parameter pollution (send confirmed twice).
